title: A little Easter color.
summary: An Easter family visit to Berlin Farms in Massachusetts: colorful eggs, an enthusiastic bunny, wide-open fields and a few practical notes before you go.
search: The journalBerlin, MassachusettsAn Easter field note The bunny had a few photo ideas of its own. A spring visit to Berlin FarmsA little Easter color.An egg hunt, a bunny with a few good poses, and a family photograph worth keeping.An AUsome Life · Published October 7, 2026 From an earlier Easter visitPastel eggs across the lawn. White fences beyond the buildings. One orange jacket that had apparently declined the pastel dress code.Our Easter photographs from Berlin Farms deserved a little space in the journal. Opened from the family albumThe eggs were everywhere.There is a particular sort of New England spring photograph: green beginning to return to the grass, bare trees in the distance, and everybody sensibly still wearing a jacket. Our Berlin Farms pictures have all of that, with the addition of a lawn covered in pink, yellow, blue and green eggs.A canvas shopping bag is ready for the egg hunt. The Easter Bunny has a pink bow, a floral backdrop, and considerably more enthusiasm for posing than most adults can sustain. I especially like the photograph with the arms up. There is plenty happening in it, and that smile is the part I keep coming back to.Then there is the family picture: the three of us together, the bunny at one end, and the stone patio beneath our feet. I am glad we have that one. A canvas tote, a lawn full of eggs, and a very visible orange jacket.All of us in the frame. The bunny makes four. A little spring color. Original editorial illustration.Between the photographsA little room to look around.The farm makes a lovely setting for this chapter. White clapboard buildings sit beside lines of white fencing, with fields stretching beyond them. In one photograph, a horse is grazing in the distance. The colors are mostly green, white and gray, which leaves the orange jacket with very little competition.I like having a wider view among the close-ups. It brings back the shape of a place: the deck, the fence, the buildings around the egg-hunt lawn. A family album needs a little of the scenery, too. White fences, open fields, and a sky still considering its spring options. One for the albumThe good part is right here.The photographs beside the black door are worth keeping in the set. There is a cap being adjusted, a yellow egg on the grass, and four very large letters spelling LOVE. The farm has helpfully supplied the caption.A tote bag, a bunny, and a few photographs I am glad we took.That is what I want to keep from this Easter visit: the color on the lawn, the bunny pictures, and our family together in the middle of it.One more photograph beside the LOVE door. title: A little Bristol blue.
summary: A family photograph from Bristol, Rhode Island, a short waterfront guide, and our experience practicing staying together safely.
search: The journalBristol, Rhode IslandFrom the family archives · October 19, 2026 An afternoon by the harborA little Bristol blue.Sailboats, stripes, and a much smaller James. A photograph from the family album, with a short guide for an afternoon on the waterfront.Looking through old photos and found this one. Apparently, we all got the memo about wearing blue.The three of us by the water. From an earlier family visit. Glad we took this one.Bristol, Rhode Island: sailboats, sparkling water, and a family afternoon by the harbor. There is James in front, with the boats behind us and the sun on the water.There is a practical detail in the photograph, too. James and I were each holding a voluntary walking handle as we practiced staying together safely. Nothing was attached to him; there was no tether or restraint, and he could let go at any time.For our family, it was one way to practice while getting out and enjoying the community. Every child and family has different needs, and what worked for us may not feel right or be appropriate for someone else. It was one small part of our experience, alongside close supervision.Mostly, I am glad we have this picture. An afternoon by the water with my two favorite people. Original editorial illustration, inspired by Bristol. An imagined harbor scene, separate from our family photograph. A small plan for a day outAlong the waterfront.These are researched ideas for a visit today, rather than a list of places we visited on the afternoon in our photograph.Start at Independence Park.At 419–459 Thames Street, this four-acre park overlooks Bristol Harbor and marks the southern end of the East Bay Bike Path. The state tourism listing includes walkways and public restrooms; check restroom availability for your visit. A good starting point for watching the boats without committing to a long walk.Independence Park visitor informationTake a waterfront wander.The town points visitors to the boardwalk behind Stone Harbour condominiums, leading toward Rockwell Park and the Maritime Center. Choose a short stretch, stop for the view, and turn back whenever you like.Bristol’s official places guideTry a little of the bike path.The East Bay Bike Path runs 13.8 miles between Providence and Bristol. You do not have to tackle the whole thing: a short out-and-back from Independence Park can be enough. Cyclists share the path, so plan the support and space your family needs.East Bay Bike Path detailsMake Audubon a separate stop.The Audubon Nature Center and Aquarium at 1401 Hope Street has exhibits, walking trails and a boardwalk toward Narragansett Bay. Audubon describes its facility and trails as accessible. Check opening hours, admission and closure announcements before heading over.Audubon visitor informationBefore you go: check parking signs, restroom access and waterfront conditions. Bristol announced funding for seawall work at Independence Park and the Maritime Center in October 2026; the notice does not establish a closure schedule, so check local updates before visiting. Waterfront routes can include open edges, docks and boat activity.Official visitor sources checked October 19, 2026. This is a family recollection with a researched guide, not a current accessibility audit. Town seawall project notice. About the walking handle & practicing staying together safelyWe each held part of the handle, with James choosing to hold his. It gave us a way to practice walking together. Unexpected separation can become dangerous quickly, even with attentive caregivers.A similar style is called Hold-On Handles. This link shows the type of product, not a confirmed match for ours; current stock and suitability need checking.In a 2012 parent survey involving 1,218 autistic children, 49% were reported to have attempted elopement at least once after age four. That describes the surveyed group, not any individual child’s future. Read the original study in Pediatrics.The practical, hopeful part is making room for learning and finding supports that fit. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends teaching safety skills alongside consistent adult supervision and an individual safety plan. Read the AAP’s guidance for families.A voluntarily held handle can be released at any moment. It cannot prevent unexpected separation or replace close supervision, particularly near water or traffic. We are sharing our experience, not general advice or a recommendation for restraint. Neither source establishes that a walking handle reduces elopement.Different people need different supports. For us, the point was getting out together and having opportunities to practice. Share this storySend a little Bristol to someone.Know someone who would enjoy an afternoon by the harbor? title: A little 1954 magic in Buenos Aires.
summary: Photos of Don Julio in Palermo, Buenos Aires, and the sweet 1954 tradition Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve share before their Viking cruise.
search: Buenos Aires, Argentina · From the family camera rollA little 1954 magic in Buenos Aires.Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve, a famous restaurant, and a very special number.A family travel note · October 2026One happy stop in Buenos Aires before the next adventure at sea. Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve are off on another adventure! Before boarding their Viking cruise, they made a stop at Don Julio in Buenos Aires — a restaurant recommended by my colleagues in Argentina.And what a gorgeous place for a photograph. Green-and-white striped awnings, a beautiful old building, and pumpkins everywhere. They look almost like New England in October, even though it's spring in Buenos Aires.But one of my favorite pictures from this stop isn't of the restaurant at all. Another 1954 for their collection.Their little travel tradition1954.Mom-Mom and Steve were both born in 1954. Wherever they travel, if they spot that number on a building, sign, or street address, they take a photograph.A small souvenir from every place they find it. I love that they have this tradition — a little reminder of the year they both came into the world.Of all the things you can collect while traveling, I think this might be one of the sweetest. ❤️ A little adventure of their own.These two give so much love and time to James and their other grandchildren. They're part of the family village that makes so many of our days possible, particularly when life involves the extra planning and support James needs.They also love to travel. And I love seeing them out exploring together, doing something for themselves, collecting stories (and 1954s) along the way.Oh, and don't worry: Ruby was in very good hands while they were away. 🐾 The Don Julio storefront on a beautiful sunny day.Pumpkins in springtime, Buenos Aires style. A little connection back homeA taste of Argentina, by way of Maine.Speaking of Buenos Aires: if you'd like a taste of Argentina a little closer to home, Rococo Ice Cream in Kennebunk, Maine, has its own Argentine connection. Its founder spent time in Argentina, where the city's ice-cream culture helped inspire what became one of our family's favorite New England stops.Read our family's Rococo story, A scoop with a view → We have lots more to share from Mom-Mom and Steve's South American travels. For now, here's to a beautiful stop at Don Julio, a recommendation from colleagues halfway around the world, and another little piece of 1954 to add to the collection.May they find a thousand more. ❤️❤️ The 1954 photo tradition Have you ever found your year? Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve look for 1954 wherever they go. An old doorway, a date carved into a building, a street number in another country. It is such a little thing, and such a lovely way to remember a place. Were you born in 1954, too? Have you ever stopped to photograph your own birth year, an anniversary or another number that means something to you? I'd love to hear what you've found. title: Burlington, at our pace.
summary: Our Burlington, Vermont trip in family photographs: Oakledge’s accessible treehouse, pool time at The Essex, Al’s French Frys, and a little holiday sparkle.
search: Burlington & Essex, Vermont · From the family album Burlington, at our pace. A treehouse, a swim, a stop at Al’s, and a little holiday sparkle. The small pieces of a Vermont trip worth keeping. Published October 16, 2026 · Photographs from an earlier family trip Pool time at The Essex. One of the good parts of getting away. Looking back through our Burlington photographs, I keep coming back to the smaller scenes: James in his Vermont shirt, the red booths at Al’s, a tree growing straight through a treehouse, and the two of them together in the pool. There is a very good Vermont trip in those pictures. A little time outside. Something familiar to eat. Water to get into. A Christmas tree dressed in black-and-white checks, because apparently even the decorations had packed appropriately. For our family, those ordinary pieces deserve room in the story. James loves the water, and the swimming photographs belong right alongside the sightseeing ones. The pool is part of the trip. A swim at The Essex The indoor pool at The Essex Resort & Spa has a lovely setting: wood walls, white beams, large windows, and blue-green water. In our photographs, James is wearing his life jacket with his dad beside him. In another, the two of them are wrapped up in a poolside hug. The photograph I would keep even without a travel story attached.White robes, white columns, and a little Vermont sunshine. The covered walkway is another detail I like in the album: two white robes, a long row of columns, and stripes of sunlight across the path. It is a useful reminder to ask about the journey between a room and a pool. The Essex’s spa is in a separate building; the practical notes below include the resort’s current access information. A treehouse you can actually get into At Oakledge Park in Burlington, the treehouse is built around the tree itself. Thick branches frame the view; the floorboards and rustic railings make a little room in the woods. James’s orange jacket stands out against all that weathered wood. Inside Oakledge’s treehouse, with the tree very much part of the room.A place to stop and look out. The access is part of what makes this place worth knowing about. Its builders describe it as a universally accessible community treehouse, created with the City of Burlington. That matters: the experience of being up among the branches should have room for more people. Our photographs capture the inside, rather than the full approach. For a future visit, I would check the route and current conditions with the park, especially after wet or icy weather. A lovely wooden walkway still has to contend with Vermont. Red booths and a Vermont shirt Our stop at Al’s French Frys in South Burlington looks exactly like the sort of place you hope to find on a New England trip: red booths, little pendant lights, and a black-and-white tiled floor. James is standing by the table in his Vermont shirt, with his device close by. A Vermont shirt for a Vermont stop. Al’s French Frys, South Burlington. That is a useful little travel detail in its own right. A communication device belongs at the table, within reach. New surroundings need not mean leaving familiar supports behind. Al’s current menu lists its namesake fries alongside burgers, sandwiches, and ice cream. The photo is our souvenir of the stop; for a particular food preference or allergy, check the current menu and preparation details directly. A little holiday sparkle A grin, red ornaments, and rather good checked ribbon. And then there is this picture. James, smiling beside the Christmas tree, blue Crocs and all. The ribbon is coordinated. The family travel wardrobe is taking a more independent approach. Looking through this trip again, what stands out is the variety without the need for a grand production: the treehouse, the pool, the diner, the decorations. There is plenty here for a family album, and plenty to build a manageable Burlington visit around. Take the useful details with youPlanning your own version These are memories from an earlier trip. The venue details below were checked on October 16, 2026; they describe what the venues currently publish, rather than facilities we personally tested. The Essex Resort & Spa · 70 Essex Way, EssexThe resort lists a year-round indoor pool. Its accessibility page says the spa and fitness center are in a separate building with paved wheelchair access, and that the pools and whirlpool have lifts. Ask about the exact route from your room, lift availability, changing arrangements, and current family swimming hours. We did not test the lifts or accessible rooms. Oakledge Park · Flynn Avenue, BurlingtonThe treehouse is documented as a universally accessible community treehouse. Burlington’s parks guidance says it is first come, first served and must remain open to the public. Burlington Wildways lists parking and accessible spaces near the Greenway. Check current parking charges, restroom availability, and the condition of the treehouse approach before you go. Al’s French Frys · 1251 Williston Road, South BurlingtonOur photo shows indoor booth seating. It does not establish wheelchair clearance, restroom access, or typical sound levels. Call 802-862-9203 for the seating or access details your family needs, and check the current menu and hours. A simple plan Choose one main outing, leave room for swimming, and keep a food stop flexible. These places are in Burlington, South Burlington, and Essex, so allow for driving between them. The photographs are a collection of trip moments, not a timed itinerary. For us, a useful planning question is: what does everyone need in order to enjoy the part we came for? A place to change, a device within reach, time to linger, and permission to finish while the day is still going well. Our hotel and pool checklist can help with the calls before booking.
